brief: The CBOT Treasury bond futures contract has turned negatively convex because its cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) bond shifts via a fixed conversion-factor table that ignores yield level. With the 20Y near 5.68%, the CTD duration is 13.24, up 20% in weeks; if the 20Y crosses 6%, the CTD could extend past 17 years, forcing hedging equivalent to $110bn of new 20Y supply over four months. This is pro-cyclical: falling bond prices lengthen CTD duration, triggering hedge selling that pushes rates higher and extends CTD again. CFTC data show asset managers already cutting bullish ultra-long futures positions (~$38bn 10Y-equivalent over two weeks to Oct 6, net long smallest since September 2025) and falling open interest. Basis traders (an $830bn position) could be squeezed next, selling cash Treasuries if volatility rises further. Goldman's William Marshall argues the convexity amplifier is mostly spent and recommends adding duration; the author sides with Bassman, noting the next 35bps would add more duration (3.6 years) than the last 70bps did (2.2 years). Bassman frames the move as a fiscal-trust problem, not a monetary one, citing a 2.90% TIPS real rate.
